teaser: A poster that made its painter famous overnight, and turned street advertising into art.
review_notes:
About 3,000 copies posted in Paris in late 1891.
Size about 190 x 117 cm, printed from several stones on joined sheets; the complete poster has an additional top strip repeating the name a third time, which this impression does not show.
Four colors: black, yellow, red, blue (the gray of Valentin is a spattered blue-black tone); lesson speaks only of 'a handful of colors'.
Spatter technique (crachis) with a brush or toothbrush.
La Goulue = Louise Weber, 'the glutton', nickname from emptying customers' glasses; kicked hats off with her foot; died 1929 in poverty.
Valentin le Désossé (Jacques Renaudin), by day said to work in the wine trade.
Earlier Moulin Rouge poster by Jules Chéret (1889).
Lautrec made about thirty posters in ten years.
Collectors peeling posters off walls at night.

lesson.text: You are walking down a Paris boulevard in December 1891, in a hurry, in the cold. A sheet of paper on a wall has about two seconds to stop you. What would it need to show?

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec's answer was this: a dancer's raised leg, a strange gray man in the way, and the name of a dance hall shouted more than once. He was 27 and had never designed a poster before. Within days, everyone in Paris knew his name.

The Moulin Rouge, two years old, wanted to advertise its star. She was Louise Weber, known as La Goulue, “the glutton”, supposedly because she drained customers' glasses as she danced past their tables. Her partner was a tall, rubber-limbed man called Valentin le Désossé, “the boneless”.
La Goulue's signature move was a high kick that knocked the top hat off a man in the audience. Valentin danced for pleasure, not pay: he is said to have had a day job in the wine trade.
Lautrec did not draw the dance hall. He boiled it down to three layers, set one behind the other like sheets of cut paper, and let the eye do the rest.

lesson.title: Three layers
lesson.text: Front, middle, back. Each is handled in a different way.

spots.title: Valentin, up front
spots.text: The nearest figure is a flat gray-violet shape with a top hat, a jutting chin and one hand raised. He is cut off by the bottom and right edges, as if he had just stepped in front of you.

spots.title: La Goulue, in the middle
spots.text: She spins away from us, blond topknot, red polka-dot blouse, one red stocking kicking. Her swirling petticoats are not white ink. They are the bare paper, with a few lines for the frills.

spots.title: The crowd, behind
spots.text: The audience is one continuous black cutout. No faces, only the outlines of top hats and feathered bonnets. You recognize the Paris public by its hats alone.

lesson.text: Nothing here is shaded to look round. There are a handful of flat colors, heavy outlines, and a floor whose boards rush off at an angle. Lautrec learned this from Japanese woodblock prints, which were cheap and popular in Paris and which treated a picture as flat shapes fitted together.
A poster has to be read at a distance and at speed. Lautrec understood that leaving things out, such as faces, shadows and details, makes an image hit harder.

The technique was color lithography: the artist draws with a greasy crayon on a slab of limestone, the stone is inked, and the ink sticks only where the grease is. Each color needs its own stone and its own pass through the press. This poster was too big for one sheet, around 1.9 meters tall (over 6 feet), so it was printed in sections and joined.
The grainy mist on Valentin's body is spatter. Lautrec loaded a stiff brush with ink and flicked it over the stone, a trick that gave him soft tone without a single painted gradation.

The lettering is part of the design too. “Moulin Rouge” is stacked in red, sharing one giant M, so the name drums like a chorus. The artist put his own name on the sheet as well, the way a painter signs a canvas.
Lautrec signed the poster by hand on the stone. Where is his signature?

spots.title: “HLautrec”
spots.text: At the lower left, on the dance floor, a slanted handwritten H and “Lautrec”. Signing an advertisement was a statement: this is my work, not anonymous commercial printing.

lesson.text: The printer's name sits at the opposite corner, in small type. About three thousand copies were pasted across the city. Collectors soon wanted them so badly that some were peeled off the walls at night before the glue had dried.
La Goulue outlived her fame. She grew too heavy to dance, ran a fairground booth, worked as a lion tamer, and ended up selling peanuts and matches near the Moulin Rouge. She died in 1929.

Lautrec made about thirty posters in the ten years he had left. They are the reason a concert flyer, a film poster or an album cover can be taken seriously as art. And the one in front of you was never meant to last longer than the rain on a Paris wall.

quiz.question: What are La Goulue's white petticoats made of in the poster?
quiz.explanation: Lautrec left the paper blank and added only a few lines for the frills.

quiz.question: How is the audience shown?
options: As a single black silhouette of hats
As detailed portraits of famous Parisians
It is not shown at all
quiz.explanation: The crowd is one black cutout, recognizable by its top hats and bonnets.

quiz.question: In color lithography, why does each color need a separate stone?
options: Because the stones wear out after one print
Because each stone is inked with one color and printed in its own pass
quiz.explanation: Every color is drawn on its own stone and printed separately.

quiz.question: How did Lautrec create the grainy tone on Valentin's body?
options: By spattering ink from a stiff brush
By gluing sand to the paper
By rubbing the print with charcoal
quiz.explanation: He flicked ink over the stone to get a soft mist of dots.

quiz.question: What does the nickname “La Goulue” mean?
quiz.explanation: She was said to empty customers' glasses as she danced past.

facts.text: This was the first poster Lautrec ever designed.
facts.explanation: He was 27 and had never made one before; it made him famous within days.

facts.text: The figure in the foreground is the owner of the Moulin Rouge.
facts.explanation: He is Valentin le Désossé, La Goulue's dance partner.

facts.text: Lautrec left the poster unsigned because it was only an advertisement.
facts.explanation: He signed it at the lower left, claiming it as his own work.
